questions.question: A large square is one whole. It is divided into 100 equal parts, and 9 of those parts are shaded. Which decimal names the shaded amount?
questions.explain: 9 out of 100 equal parts is 9/100, and hundredths need two places after the point, so it is 0.09. The trap is copying the digit 9 straight behind the point and writing 0.9, which means 9 tenths — ten times too much.

questions.question: A number line from 0 to 1 is cut into 1000 equal steps. A dot sits on the 47th step. Which decimal shows where the dot is?
questions.explain: 47 of 1000 equal steps is 47/1000, and thousandths need three places after the point, so 0.047. Watch out for just copying the digits 47 behind the point: 0.47 is 47 hundredths, which sits ten times farther along the line.

questions.question: A paper strip is one whole. It is folded into 10 equal parts and 8 of the parts are coloured. Which pair names the coloured amount correctly?
questions.explain: 8 of 10 equal parts is 8/10, and tenths take one place after the point, so 8/10 = 0.8. The common trap is copying both numbers of the fraction into the decimal, like the one that says 8.10 — the denominator tells you the place value, it is not a digit to copy.

questions.question: A metre stick is one whole. It is divided into 1000 equal millimetre parts, and 250 of those parts are covered with tape. Which decimal names the taped amount?
questions.explain: 250 of 1000 equal parts is 250/1000 = 0.250, which is the same as 0.25. If you count places carelessly you can slide the digits one place too far right and get 0.025, which is only 25 thousandths.

questions.question: Which fraction names the same amount as the decimal 0.406?
questions.explain: The last digit of 0.406 sits in the thousandths place, so the whole is cut into 1000 parts and the decimal is 406/1000. A common slip is ignoring the zero in the middle and reading it as 46 thousandths.

questions.question: Sofia is filling in a place-value chart. One row shows the decimal 0.070. Which fraction belongs beside it?
questions.explain: 0.070 ends in the thousandths place, so it is 70/1000 (the same amount as 7/100). The trap is matching the digits 70 to the denominator 100 and writing 70/100, which is really 0.7 — ten times bigger.

questions.question: In science class, Liam measured a maple leaf and found it was 85/1000 of a metre long. Which decimal should he write in his data table?
questions.explain: A denominator of 1000 means thousandths, so the last digit must land three places after the point: 85/1000 = 0.085. Copying the digits 85 right behind the point gives 0.85, which would be a leaf ten times longer.

questions.question: Maya's ribbon is 0.6 m long. She wants to record the length as a fraction with a denominator of 100. Which fraction should she write?
questions.explain: 0.6 is 6 tenths, and each tenth is 10 hundredths, so 0.6 = 60/100. The trap is copying the digit 6 onto the new denominator and writing 6/100, which is only 0.06 m — about the width of a finger.

questions.question: Ryan wrote this in his notebook: 7/1000 = 0.7. Which statement is correct?
options: Ryan is wrong: 7/1000 = 0.007, because the 7 belongs in the thousandths place.
Ryan is right, because the fraction and the decimal both use the digit 7.
questions.explain: The denominator 1000 tells you the last digit sits three places after the point, so 7/1000 = 0.007. Ryan copied the digit 7 straight behind the point; 0.7 is 700/1000, which is one hundred times bigger.

questions.question: During the Terry Fox run at school, Ava ran 0.75 km before her first water break and Noah ran 8/10 km. Which statement is true?
options: Ava ran farther, because 8/10 km = 0.08 km, and 0.75 > 0.08.
Noah ran farther, because 8/10 km = 0.80 km, and 0.80 > 0.75.
Noah ran farther, because 8/10 km = 8.10 km, and 8.10 > 0.75.
They ran the same distance, because 8/10 km = 0.75 km exactly.
questions.explain: First change the fraction to a decimal: 8/10 = 0.8 = 0.80, then compare hundredths — 80 hundredths beats 75 hundredths, so Noah ran farther. The traps are copying the digits into 8.10 or sliding the 8 into the hundredths place as 0.08.

questions.question: The label on Jasmine's water bottle says it holds 500/1000 L. She says the same amount can be written in other ways. Which list gives three names for the SAME amount?
questions.explain: 500/1000 = 0.500, and stripping the end zeros gives 0.5 = 5/10 = 50/100, so all three names match. A common error is gluing the digits of the fraction together as 0.510, or dropping the 5 into the hundredths place as 5/100 = 0.05.

questions.question: Owen measured the snow on his deck in Prince George as 3/100 of a metre deep. On his weather chart he wrote 0.3 m instead. How much deeper does his chart make the snow look than it really is?
options: 0 m, because 3/100 and 0.3 name the same amount
questions.explain: The real depth is 3/100 = 0.03 m, so the error is 0.3 - 0.03 = 0.27 m. The trap is believing 3/100 and 0.3 are the same because they share the digit 3 — the denominator 100 puts the 3 in the hundredths place, ten times smaller.
